title: What Does BERT with Vision Look At?
abstract: Pre-trained visually grounded language models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT, and UNITER have achieved significant performance improvement on vision-and-language tasks but what they learn during pre-training remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate that certain attention heads of a visually grounded language model actively ground elements of language to image regions. Specifically, some heads can map entities to image regions, performing the task known as entity grounding. Some heads can even detect the syntactic relations between non-entity words and image regions, tracking, for example, associations between verbs and regions corresponding to their arguments. We denote this ability as syntactic grounding. We verify grounding both quantitatively and qualitatively, using Flickr30K Entities as a testbed.
research_question: What do visually grounded language models learn during pre-training? Specifically, do they learn to ground language to image regions?
core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that certain attention heads in visually grounded language models actively ground entities and syntactic relations to image regions, and this grounding improves in higher layers.
conclusion: The paper concludes that visually grounded language models learn to ground language to image regions through attention heads, and this grounding is linguistically inspired, suggesting potential for further analysis of cross-modal models.
key_findings: Some attention heads perform entity grounding with high accuracy, significantly above a rule-based baseline.
Some heads perform syntactic grounding, linking non-entity words to image regions based on syntactic dependencies.
Grounding accuracy increases in higher layers, indicating refinement of understanding over layers.
The model exhibits cross-modal pronoun resolution (e.g., 'her' resolved to woman).
The grounding behavior is linguistically inspired, resembling entity coreference resolution and syntactic parsing.
future_direction: It would be interesting to see if more linguistically-inspired phenomena can be systematically found in cross-modal models.
